q: A lab technician mixes freshly collected sperm with an oocyte in plain salt solution. The sperm swim vigorously for hours, but none gets through the zona pellucida. The same sperm succeed after a few hours in a medium containing albumin, bicarbonate and calcium. What did the second medium allow?
options: Capacitation
The cortical reaction
Completion of meiosis II in the sperm
Formation of the acrosome
misconception: sperm can fertilize as soon as they are ejaculated

q: Put the steps of fertilization in order, starting when sperm reach the uterine tube.
options: Sperm capacitate over several hours
Capacitated sperm push through the corona radiata
The acrosomal reaction releases enzymes that digest a path through the zona pellucida
One sperm fuses with the oocyte's plasma membrane
Calcium waves trigger the cortical reaction
The oocyte completes meiosis II, and the chromosomes of the two pronuclei combine into the zygote

q: Name the pinned layer.
options: Corona radiata
Zona pellucida
Oocyte plasma membrane
Acrosome

Top right: the same view, with holes opening in the pink layer as sperm release enzymes against the clear band. Bottom, an enlarged boxed view: several sperm tunnel through the pink cell layer; their caps of enzymes are released at the clear band; one sperm has crossed the band and its head has merged with the oocyte's membrane, its nucleus entering the yellow cytoplasm. Labels mark the acrosome, sperm nucleus, oocyte cytoplasm, plasma membrane, sperm-binding proteins in that membrane, the clear band and the outer cell layer.

q: Name the pinned layer.

Theca
Zona pellucida
Cortical granules

q: In a lab experiment, a drug stops cortical granules from fusing with the oocyte's plasma membrane but has no other effect. A sperm fuses with the oocyte. Predict each variable compared with an untreated oocyte.

variables.name: Calcium waves in the oocyte after fusion
Cutting of ZP2 in the zona pellucida
Number of sperm able to bind the zona after the first sperm enters

q: A man's sperm cannot swim well, so his partner's oocytes are fertilized by intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), in which one sperm is injected directly into the oocyte's cytoplasm. Select every step that ICSI bypasses.
options: Crossing the corona radiata
The acrosomal reaction
Calcium waves in the oocyte
Crossing the zona pellucida
Completion of meiosis II
Fusion of the sperm and oocyte membranes

q: A couple has intercourse once, on day 11 of a 28-day cycle, and the woman ovulates on day 14. She becomes pregnant. Which statement best explains how?
options: The oocyte waited in the uterine tube from day 11 until the sperm reached it there
Some sperm survived in her tract for three days and fertilized the oocyte after ovulation
Fertilization happened on day 11, and the zygote then paused in the tube until day 14
Sperm entered the ovary and fertilized the oocyte inside its follicle

q: A zygote has the sex chromosomes XY. Where did its Y chromosome come from?
options: The secondary oocyte
The second polar body
The sperm
Either gamete, with equal chance

q: A student wrote out the events that follow sperm entry. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: The sperm delivers an enzyme that starts calcium waves in the oocyte
Cortical granules release their contents under the zona pellucida
The oocyte, released from its pause, completes meiosis I
A second polar body is pinched off
Two haploid pronuclei form and copy their DNA

q: Complete the sequence: sperm capacitate → sperm cross the corona radiata → ____ → sperm cross the zona pellucida → one sperm fuses with the oocyte.
options: The acrosomal reaction
The cortical reaction
The second polar body forms
Pronuclei form

q: Select every mechanism that keeps a second sperm out of a human oocyte after the first one fuses.
options: An enzyme from the cortical granules cuts the zona protein that sperm bind
The zona pellucida stiffens
The oocyte membrane sheds the receptor protein sperm use to bind it
The corona radiata cells close ranks and seal the path
The second polar body plugs the entry site

q: A man's semen has normal numbers of sperm that swim well, but every sperm has a round head with no acrosome. In the lab, his sperm reach the zona pellucida of donor oocytes but never get through. Which approach can bypass the problem?
options: Giving him testosterone to make more sperm
Placing many more of his sperm around each oocyte
Injecting one sperm directly into each oocyte
Adding extra albumin and calcium to capacitate his sperm

q: After a pelvic infection, both of a woman's uterine tubes are scarred shut near the uterus. She still ovulates every month. Why can she not become pregnant without treatment?
options: Her oocytes can no longer complete meiosis I before they are released
Her ovaries stop releasing oocytes once the tubes are blocked
Scarring prevents capacitation in the uterus
Sperm cannot get past the blockage to the ampulla, where fertilization happens

q: Sperm spend several hours in the fluid of the uterine tube. Predict the change in each variable in a typical sperm by the end of that time.

variables.name: Cholesterol in the sperm's plasma membrane
Number of chromosomes in the sperm

q: What is a zygote?
options: The diploid cell formed when the chromosomes of a sperm and an oocyte combine
A secondary oocyte that has been released at ovulation and is paused at metaphase II
A sperm that has finished capacitation in the uterine tube and can now fertilize
The small cell that holds discarded chromosomes from meiosis II

q: An early pregnancy loss is examined, and its cells contain 69 chromosomes: two paternal sets and one maternal set. Which failure best explains this?
options: Nondisjunction of one chromosome pair during the father's meiosis
The oocyte skipped meiosis I
The zygote copied all of its DNA twice before it first divided
Two sperm entered the oocyte: the block to polyspermy failed

q: An experimental contraceptive vaccine makes a woman produce antibodies that coat ZP2 in the zona pellucida of her oocytes. Which step of fertilization would it block?
options: Sperm binding to the zona pellucida
Capacitation of sperm in her tract
Calcium waves after sperm fusion
Completion of meiosis II

q: Why are a person's mitochondria inherited from the mother only?
options: The sperm's mitochondria enter the oocyte but are marked and destroyed
Sperm have no mitochondria
The sperm's midpiece and its mitochondria stay outside the zona pellucida
Mitochondria are built from scratch in the zygote using its nuclear DNA

q: A woman who is trying to conceive has a sensitive blood test for hCG five days after she ovulated. It is negative, but a repeat test a week later is positive. Assuming she conceived on the day of ovulation, why was the first test negative?
options: Her corpus luteum had not yet started to make hCG in amounts a test can detect
The embryo had not yet implanted
hCG is made only once the embryo's heart begins to beat
The zygote's hCG was still trapped inside the zona pellucida
misconception: hCG is made from fertilization onward

q: Put the stages from zygote to implantation in order.
options: The zygote divides into two blastomeres
A solid morula of about 16 to 32 cells forms
A fluid-filled blastocoel forms, making a blastocyst
The blastocyst hatches from the zona pellucida
The blastocyst attaches to the endometrium, inner cell mass side first
The syncytiotrophoblast invades the endometrium and secretes hCG

q: Name the pinned part of the blastocyst.
options: Trophoblast
Blastocoel
Inner cell mass
Morula

q: Name the pinned layer of the blastocyst.
options: Trophoblast
Zona pellucida
Inner cell mass
Epiblast

fig.alt: A drawing of an ovary, a uterine tube and part of the uterus, with seven numbered boxes (1 to 6, with 5 used twice) connected by arrows to points along the tube. variables.name: Survival of the corpus luteum past its usual two weeks
Chance that the endometrium is shed
Intensity of a home pregnancy test line

q: Select every tissue that develops from mesoderm.
options: Skeletal muscle
Epidermis
Dermis
Lining of the stomach
Cardiac muscle
Bone

q: An X-ray of a newborn shows one wedge-shaped, half-formed thoracic vertebra with a missing rib on the same side. The overlying skin and back muscles are normal. Which part of the embryo most likely developed abnormally?
options: The myotome of one somite
The neural crest at that level
The apical ectodermal ridge
The sclerotome of one somite

q: A tumor arises from the epithelial cells lining the pancreatic ducts. From which germ layer did those cells originally develop?
options: Ectoderm
Mesoderm
Endoderm
Neural crest

q: A student outlined how an implanting embryo prevents a menstrual period. One step is wrong. Which one?

hCG binds FSH receptor proteins on the growing follicles
The corpus luteum survives past its usual 12 to 14 days
Progesterone secretion continues
The endometrium is kept intact and not shed

q: In a chick embryo experiment, the apical ectodermal ridge is removed from a wing bud after the upper wing has formed but before the rest has. What does the wing look like when the chick hatches?
options: A normal, full-length wing
No wing at all
An upper wing but no lower wing or wing tip
A wing tip attached directly to the body

variables.name: Sodium pumped into the center of the morula

options: Notochord
Primitive streak
Neural tube
Hypoblast

options: Chorion
Yolk sac

q: A pathologist tests cells from each embryonic membrane of an early pregnancy for human chorionic gonadotropin. In which membrane will she find the cells that make it?
options: Amnion
Chorion
Yolk sac

Missing fingers

Embryonic disc
Neural tube

q: In the late 1950s, a sedative given to pregnant women caused severe limb defects. Babies were affected when their mothers took it between about days 20 and 36 after fertilization, but not when it was first taken in week 12. What best explains the difference?
options: By week 12 the zona pellucida protects the fetus
By week 12 the mother's liver had adapted to break the drug down before it reached the fetus
The limbs form during weeks 4 to 8, so by week 12 they were already formed
Drugs cannot reach the fetus after the end of week 8

Extra toes on the foot of the same leg
An unusually long femur

In the epithelium lining the gut

Trachea

q: Why do your knees face forward while your elbows point backward?

The leg buds formed on the front of the body and the arm buds on the back

Warfarin cannot dissolve clots in pregnant women
Heparin crosses the placenta and protects the fetus from clots
Heparin does not cross the placenta in useful amounts

options: Week 4
Week 10
Week 24
Week 40

Progesterone starts at about 10 percent, stays nearly flat until about week 10, then climbs steadily to its peak at week 40. q: A baby is born at 27 weeks of pregnancy. Within hours, her breathing is fast and labored and her lungs are stiff. Her mother had not received any drug before the birth. What is the most likely reason?

They remove carbon dioxide from the fetal blood

They pump blood through the ductus arteriosus

The appearance of lanugo on the fetus
The moment the fetus becomes viable
The mother's first feeling of the fetus moving

q: Two babies are born on the same day: one at 30 weeks of pregnancy, one at 41 weeks. Which description fits the baby born at 30 weeks?

Septum primum
Endocardial cushion
Foramen ovale

The uterus pressed on the aorta and raised afterload
Lying down triggered a vagal reflex that stopped the heart
Blood pooled in her lungs when she lay flat on the table

options: About 14%
About 20%
About 33%
About 50%

About 108 mm Hg
About 88 mm Hg
About 63 mm Hg

Plasma rose more than red cell mass

Respiratory acidosis from the uterus pressing on the diaphragm

An ectopic pregnancy in a scarred tube

An ultrasound to find where the placenta lies
A digital examination of the cervix
Placing an intravenous line

He inherited type 1 diabetes and makes no insulin
Her insulin crossed the placenta and is still acting on him
His liver cannot yet store any glycogen for use after birth

q: Screening for gestational diabetes is done at weeks 24 to 28, not at the first visit. Why does the condition usually appear in the second half of pregnancy?

The mother's pancreas shrinks as the growing uterus presses on it

Insulin-resisting placental hormones rise

Widening of the ureters
A rise in clotting factors made by the liver
Slower movement through the gut
Growth of the uterine smooth muscle

Creatinine cannot be measured accurately in pregnancy

Estrogen weakens the bladder's lining
Pregnant women empty the bladder less often

q: The pinned outline shows the height of the uterus at the end of which trimester?

End of the second trimester
End of the third trimester
Before pregnancy

The poorly supplied placenta releases factors that block vessel growth
The mother's endothelium is damaged throughout her body
Her arterioles dilate, lowering total peripheral resistance

Placental abruption
An ectopic pregnancy
Normal late-pregnancy discomfort

Her tidal volume is smaller
Smaller FRC and higher oxygen use
Her fetal hemoglobin takes oxygen from her own blood cells

The placenta receives too little maternal blood
The placenta releases factors that block blood vessel growth
The mother's endothelium is damaged throughout her body

Blood pressure rises and protein appears in her urine

In the abdominal cavity
In the cervix
In a uterine tube

Early labor, in the latent phase of the dilation stage
Lightening
The expulsion stage

The cervix reaches full dilation at 10 cm
The head crowns at the vaginal opening
The shoulders and body are delivered
The placenta shears off the shrinking uterine wall

CRH

Labor runs faster than usual, with a shorter first stage

Fatigue of the stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the cervix

Her contractions come closer together and get longer over several hours

Her cervix has thinned from 30% to 80% effaced

The placental stage
The postpartum period
The expulsion stage

Test the baby for cystic fibrosis
Tell her the risk rises only after age 35

q: A karyotype reads 47,XY,+21. What does it show?
options: A male with trisomy 21
A female with trisomy 21
A male missing chromosome 21
A male with an extra X chromosome

q: At point B, this person's resting blood tests are normal, yet a bout of pneumonia overwhelms them. What does the graph show?
options: Capacity still covers rest but not a major stress
Capacity has already fallen below the level needed at rest
The resting need has risen with age while capacity held steady
Capacity is still the same as it was at point A

fig.alt: Schematic graph of functional capacity, as a percentage of peak (0 to 100), against age (20 to 90 years). A solid curve of maximal capacity stays at 100 until age 30, then falls, slowly at first and then faster, to about 70 at 65, 55 at 80 and 44 at 90. A dashed line at 25, labeled needed at rest, stays below the curve at every age. A dashed line at 60, labeled needed during a major stress such as pneumonia, is crossed by the curve at about age 75. Point A at age 30 sits far above both lines; point B at age 80 sits above the resting line but below the stress line.

q: Why do telomeres get shorter each time most body cells divide?
options: Reactive oxygen species cut off a fixed length at every division
Telomerase removes repeats from the chromosome ends each time
Apoptosis trims the chromosome ends before each division
The polymerase cannot copy the chromosome's very end

q: Select the cells that keep their telomeres long by using telomerase.
options: Germ cells that give rise to sperm
Most cancer cells
Mature skin fibroblasts
Senescent cells
Stem cells, to a small degree

q: Normal human fibroblasts, which make almost no telomerase, are grown in a dish for many generations. Predict the change in each variable as the culture ages, compared with the start.

variables.name: Number of divisions the cells have left

q: Cellular senescence is described as double-edged. Which pair states its benefit and its cost?
options: It speeds tissue repair but uses up the stem cells
It blocks tumors but inflames nearby tissue
It lengthens telomeres but raises the risk of cancer
It removes damaged cells by apoptosis but leaves gaps

q: Mr. Hassan, 86, becomes confused over a day. His temperature is 36.9 °C, his breathing is fast, and a chest X-ray shows pneumonia. Why might he have no fever?
options: Pneumonia does not cause fever at any age
36.9 °C counts as a fever in older adults
Confusion itself lowers the body temperature set point
Fever responses are often blunted in older adults

q: Select every change expected in the cardiovascular system of a healthy, inactive 75-year-old compared with a healthy 25-year-old.
options: Higher systolic pressure
Wider pulse pressure
Lower maximum heart rate
Resting cardiac output roughly halved
More reliance on atrial contraction to fill the ventricle

q: Why does an older adult's blood pressure often read like 158/72, with a high systolic but a normal diastolic pressure?
options: A stiff aorta no longer stretches and recoils with each beat
The aging heart pumps a much larger stroke volume each beat
Arterioles relax and widen with age
Blood becomes less viscous with age

q: Mrs. Lee, 81, feels light-headed and nearly falls each time she gets out of bed. Her blood pressure drops 25 mm Hg on standing, and her heart rate barely rises. What age-related change best explains this?
options: A blunted baroreceptor reflex
Too much aldosterone
A faster SA node
Increased venous valve strength

q: A thin 84-year-old woman has a plasma creatinine in the normal range, but her calculated eGFR is 45 mL/min. How can both be true?
options: Her aging kidneys secrete creatinine faster than before
Creatinine is no longer filtered by older glomeruli
Less muscle makes less creatinine, masking a low GFR
The eGFR formula ignores age and overestimates loss

q: A drug removed from the body mainly by the kidneys is given to a 30-year-old and an 85-year-old at the same dose. What is expected in the older patient?
options: Lower blood levels from faster filtering
The same levels, set by the dose alone
No effect, from a loss of receptor proteins
Higher blood levels from slower clearance

q: Put the steps from cell division to the harm done by senescent cells in order.
options: A body cell divides many times without telomerase
Its telomeres shorten to a critical length
A telomere's cap fails and the end is read as damaged DNA
p53 and other checkpoint proteins stop the cell cycle for good
The senescent cell releases inflammatory signals into the tissue

q: A student explained why bone loss speeds up after menopause. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: The ovaries stop making estrogen
Less estrogen means osteoclasts are restrained less
Estrogen had been stimulating osteoclasts, which now slow down
Resorption outpaces formation in each remodeling cycle
Spongy bone in the vertebrae thins first

q: Fill the gap: in sarcopenia, ____ fibers shrink the most, so older muscles lose power more than endurance.
options: slow oxidative
fast glycolytic
cardiac
smooth muscle

q: Why do older adults respond less well to a new vaccine, such as one against a strain of influenza they have never met?
options: Their memory cells from past infections have all died
The shrunken thymus makes few new naive T cells
Their antibodies no longer bind antigens well
Vaccines cannot reach the lymph nodes of older adults

q: Which finding in an 80-year-old is part of normal aging rather than a disease that needs its own explanation?
options: Needing reading glasses
Dementia with memory loss
Anemia on a routine blood count
Urinary incontinence
misconception: dementia, anemia and incontinence are normal parts of aging

q: During a heat wave, Mr. Brandt, 88, who lives alone, is found confused with dry skin and a high blood sodium. Which set of age-related changes best explains why he became so ill?

Fewer sweat glands, blunted thirst, weaker urine concentration

q: Compare a healthy, inactive 80-year-old with the same person at 30. Predict the change in each variable across several systems.

variables.name: Naive T cells in the blood

q: What causes hair to turn gray with age?
options: Keratin in each hair shaft oxidizes over time
Sweat glands stop moistening the hair

q: A friend takes high-dose antioxidant supplements to slow aging. Which statement best fits the current evidence?

Reactive oxygen species play no part in aging
Trials found no benefit, and some found harm
Antioxidants lengthen telomeres in all cells

q: Residents of a nursing home, aged 86 to 96, lift weights with their legs three times a week for eight weeks. Their leg strength more than doubles. What does this show?

Strength gains in older adults come only from learning the exercise
